{{Nihongo||{{linktext|八|咫|鏡}}|'''Yata no Kagami'''}} is a sacred {{ill|bronze mirror|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/bronze mirror|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bronze mirror|qq=}} that is part of the {{ill|Imperial Regalia of Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial Regalia of Japan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Regalia of Japan|qq=}}.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cali|first1=Joseph|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J1gEEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA214|title=Shinto Shrines: A Guide to the Sacred Sites of Japan's Ancient Religion|last2=Dougill|first2=John|date=2012-11-30|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3775-4|pages=218|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Denney-2011a">{{Cite book|last=Denney|first=John W.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9ntpAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA321|title=Respect and Consideration|date=2011|publisher=Lulu.com|isbn=978-0-9568798-0-6|pages=321, 318–326|language=en}}</ref>

== Name and significance ==
The {{transliteration|ja|Yata no Kagami}} represents "wisdom" or "honesty," depending on the source.<ref name="Denney-2011a" /> Its name literally means "The Eight  Mirror," a reference to its size.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Authors|first=Various|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA127|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|pages=127|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Ponsonby-Fane|first=R. A. B.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BY23AwAAQBAJ&pg=PA108|title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines|date=2014-06-03|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-89294-3|pages=108|language=en}}</ref> Mirrors in ancient Japan represented truth because they merely reflected what was shown, and were objects of mystique and reverence (being uncommon items).

According to Shinsuke Takenaka at the Institute of Moralogy, {{transliteration|ja|Yata no Kagami}} is considered the most precious of the three sacred treasures.<ref name="bbctres">{{cite web |title=Akihito and Japan's Imperial Treasures that make a man an emperor |website=BBC |author=Anna Jones |date=27 April 2019 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-47931671 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220324032626/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-47931671 |archive-date=March 24, 2022}}</ref>

== History ==
In the year 1040 ({{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Chōkyū|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Chōkyū|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkyū|qq=}}}} 1, 9th month), the compartment which contained the Sacred Mirror was burned in a fire.<ref>Ackroyd, Joyce. (1982). ''Lessons from History: the Tokushi Yoron,'' p. 29.</ref> Whether that mirror was irrevocably lost or not, it is said to be housed today in {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ise Grand Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ise Grand Shrine|qq=}}, in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], {{ill|Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}},<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cali|first1=Joseph|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J1gEEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA214|title=Shinto Shrines: A Guide to the Sacred Sites of Japan's Ancient Religion|last2=Dougill|first2=John|date=2012-11-30|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3775-4|pages=218|language=en}}</ref> although a lack of public access makes this difficult to verify. Presently, a replica is enshrined in {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Three Palace Sanctuaries|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Palace Sanctuaries|qq=}} of the {{ill|Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial Palace|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tokyo Imperial Palace|qq=}} in Tokyo.<ref name="Denney-2011a" />

== Mythology ==
In {{ill|Shinto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto|qq=}}, the mirror was forged by the deity {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|lt=Ishikoridome|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}; both it and the {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|lt=Yasakani no magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=}}}} were hung from a tree to lure out {{ill|Amaterasu|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=}} from a cave. They were given to Amaterasu's grandson, {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=}}, when he went to pacify Japan along with the sword {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}}}}. From there, the treasures passed into the hands of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial House of Japan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial House of Japan|qq=}}.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&pg=PA4|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|pages=4–5|language=en}}</ref> The descendants of {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|lt=Ishikoridome|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}, the Kagamitsukuri created ceremonial mirrors for the Emperor when the myths were first written.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}

The double shrine complex [[Hinokuma Shrine|Hinokuma Jingu and Kunikakasu Jingu]] holds two mirrors made before this one. Prototype mirrors {{ill|Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|ja|日像鏡・日矛鏡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|qq=|1=Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11086052}} respectively.

The researcher Shinsuke Takenaka said according to the legends, Amaterasu told {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=}}: "Serve this mirror as my soul, just as you would serve me, with clean mind and body."<ref name="bbctres"/><ref name="D-2012a">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2012-02-17 |title=The circular mirror: Shinto symbol |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2012/02/18/the-circular-mirror-shinto-symbol/ |access-date=2023-12-12 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Association with the structure of the Department of divinities ==
Yata no Kagami, alongside {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|lt=Yasakani no magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=}}}} were heavily associated with Imperial ritual. Two of the main clans of the [[Department of Divinities]], the Kagamitsukuri, and the Tamatsukuri were descended from the creators of the respective artifacts: {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}, and {{ill|Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=}}. This was a part of a pattern of the clans of the Department of Divinities being descended from significant figures in the myth of Amaterasu in the cave.<ref name="hardacre-2017a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_Q81DQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto: A History|last=Hardacre|first=Helen|date=2017|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-062171-1|language=en}}</ref>{{rp|35}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}} {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}}}} is an exception, likely included to represent the submission of the [[Izumo clan]] to the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial House of Japan]].

In the [[Department of Divinities]] there was this organization.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}

* The {{ill|Inbe clan|Inbe family|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=}} was responsible for managing the procuring materials for rituals and performing abstinence rites.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} and distribution of tribute offerings within the Jingikan..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} claiming descent from Ame no [[Futodama]] no Mikoto..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}
* {{ill|Sarume clan|lt=Sarume clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|en:draft|6=ja|7=猿女君|8=fr|9=Clan Sarume|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|qq=}} women were tasked with performing sacred dances..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} Initially serving as seers and healers, their role evolved to include performing ritual dances, or kagura, during Enthronement Rites and court ceremonies..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} claiming descent from the goddess [[Ame-no-Uzume|Ame no Uzume]] no Mikoto,<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} and {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko Ōkami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko Ōkami|qq=}}. <ref name="picken-2004a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BKAhUVqKFhgC&q=Uzume&pg=PA1|title=Sourcebook in Shinto: Selected Documents|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2004|publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group|isbn=978-0-313-26432-0|language=en}}</ref><ref name="roberts-2009a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Uzume|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}}</ref><ref name="coulter-2013a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VWxekbhM1yEC&dq=Ame-no-Uzume&pg=PT91|title=Encyclopedia of Ancient Deities|last1=Coulter|first1=Charles Russell|last2=Turner|first2=Patricia|date=2013-07-04|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-135-96397-2|language=en}}</ref><ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム">{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9422|access-date=2024-03-18|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}}</ref>
* The Tamatsukuri specialized in the creation of {{ill|Magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama|qq=}}..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} and are descended from {{ill|Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=}}. <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}
* The Kagamitsukuri were known for crafting {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=bronze mirrors|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|qq=}} for use in shrine ceremonies..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} and are descended from {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}. <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}
* The {{ill|Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}} (卜部氏) considered to be of relatively low Rank, carried out divination practices..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}<ref>{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9910|access-date=2024-03-19|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}}</ref> using tortoise shells and deer [[:en:Scapula|scapulae]] <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} later taking the surname {{ill|Urabe clan|lt=Yoshida family|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}} and claiming descent from {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} alongside the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]].<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}

* [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]]: Later known as the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|lt=Fujiwara|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Fujiwara clan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujiwara clan|qq=}}, they specialized in reciting prayers to the Kami, with a divine lineage tracing back to {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}} no Mikoto..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}
** In his book ''Jinja to kodai ōken saishi'' (1989). {{ill|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iwao Ōwa|qq=}} goes on to theorize that the {{Nihongo|[[:en:Ō clan|Ō clan]]|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}} was originally {{Nihongo|ōmi|大忌|"greater taboo (priesthood)"}}, but was usurped by the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]] who were among the "lesser priesthood" (the latter claims descent from the {{Nihongo|[[Inbe clan]]|[[:ja:忌部氏|忌部氏]]}}).<ref name="gakken2">{{cite book|title=神道の本|last=小向|first=正司|publisher=学研|year=1992|series=Books Esoterica|volume=2|pages=76–7}}(zasshi code 66951-07; kyōtsu zasshi code T10-66951-07-1000)</ref>
** Takemikazuchi was originally a local god (''kuni-tsu-kami'') revered by the {{Nihongo|[[:en:Ō clan|Ō clan]]|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}},<ref name="gakken2" /> and was a god of maritime travel.<ref name="gakken2" /> However, the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]] who also has roots in this region, and when they took over control of priestly duties from the Ō clan, they also instituted Takemikazuchi as the Nakatomi clan's [[ujigami]] (clan deity). Or so this is the observation by {{ill|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iwao Ōwa|qq=}}<ref name="gakken2" />

All of these clans are descended from figures who played significant roles in the {{ill|Tenson kōrin|lt=Tenson kōrin|lt=Tenson korin|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tenson korin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenson korin|qq=}} and accompanied Ninigi during his descent, and many of them ({{ill|Sarume clan|lt=Sarume clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|en:draft|6=ja|7=猿女君|8=fr|9=Clan Sarume|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|qq=}}, {{ill|Inbe clan|Inbe family|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=}}, [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]], and {{ill|Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}}) descend from figures ([[Ame-no-Uzume|Ame no Uzume]], [[Futodama]], {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}}, and {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}} respectively) played roles in the myth of Amaterasu in the cave.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}

The {{ill|Mononobe clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Mononobe clan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mononobe clan|qq=}} considered themselves excluded from this, and their ancestor {{ill|Nigihayahi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Nigihayahi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nigihayahi|qq=}} was excluded. For this reason they wrote the {{ill|Kujiki|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kujiki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kujiki|qq=}}. They were highly influential in the development of the department of divinities, but they were not a priestly clan. The Inbe felt their role was minimized so they wrote the {{ill|Kogo Shūi|lt=Kogo Shūi|lt=Kogo Shui|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shui|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shui|qq=}} to improve their position too.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />

== Replicas in contemporary ritual ==
[[File:Masakaki with Mirror and Jewel.jpg|thumb|Right Masakaki at [[Yasaka Shrine]] featuring a Mirror and Magatama]]
[[File:Fukakusa Kaidoguchicho, Fushimi Ward, Kyoto, Kyoto Prefecture 612-0805, Japan - panoramio (1).jpg|thumb|A mirror on an altar at [[Fushimi Inari-taisha]], Yata-no-Kagami is seen as prototypical for the use of mirrors when worshipping other deities.<ref name="degaris-2013a" /><ref name="D-2012a" />]]
{{Main|Masakaki|en:Mirrors in Shinto}}
Replicas of the Imperial regalia of Japan including Yata no Kagami are included in {{ill|Masakaki|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Masakaki|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Masakaki|qq=}} at Shinto shrines.<ref name="d-2015a2">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2015-04-05 |title=The Colours of Shinto (masakaki) |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2015/04/05/the-colours-of-shinto/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref> Masakaki come in sets of two, with the left one containing a replica of {{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}} and the right one containing a replica of Yata no Kagami and {{ill|Yasakani-no-Magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yasakani-no-Magatama|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yasakani-no-Magatama|qq=}}.<ref name="d-2015a2" /> {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|qq=}} are highly significant with Yata no Kagami being seen as prototypical to them.<ref name="degaris-2013a">{{Cite book |last=De_Garis |first=Frederick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hUm0AAAAQBAJ&pg=PA237 |title=We Japanese |date=2013-09-05 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-136-18367-6 |pages=237 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="D-2012a" />

{{Nihongo||{{linktext|八|咫|鏡}}|'''Yata no Kagami'''}} is a sacred {{ill|bronze mirror|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/bronze mirror|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bronze mirror|qq=}} that is part of the {{ill|Imperial Regalia of Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial Regalia of Japan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Regalia of Japan|qq=}}.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cali|first1=Joseph|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J1gEEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA214|title=Shinto Shrines: A Guide to the Sacred Sites of Japan's Ancient Religion|last2=Dougill|first2=John|date=2012-11-30|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3775-4|pages=218|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Denney-2011a">{{Cite book|last=Denney|first=John W.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9ntpAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA321|title=Respect and Consideration|date=2011|publisher=Lulu.com|isbn=978-0-9568798-0-6|pages=321, 318–326|language=en}}</ref>

== Name and significance ==
The {{transliteration|ja|Yata no Kagami}} represents "wisdom" or "honesty," depending on the source.<ref name="Denney-2011a" /> Its name literally means "The Eight  Mirror," a reference to its size.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Authors|first=Various|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA127|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|pages=127|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Ponsonby-Fane|first=R. A. B.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BY23AwAAQBAJ&pg=PA108|title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines|date=2014-06-03|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-89294-3|pages=108|language=en}}</ref> Mirrors in ancient Japan represented truth because they merely reflected what was shown, and were objects of mystique and reverence (being uncommon items).

According to Shinsuke Takenaka at the Institute of Moralogy, {{transliteration|ja|Yata no Kagami}} is considered the most precious of the three sacred treasures.<ref name="bbctres">{{cite web |title=Akihito and Japan's Imperial Treasures that make a man an emperor |website=BBC |author=Anna Jones |date=27 April 2019 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-47931671 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220324032626/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-47931671 |archive-date=March 24, 2022}}</ref>

== History ==
In the year 1040 ({{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Chōkyū|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Chōkyū|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkyū|qq=}}}} 1, 9th month), the compartment which contained the Sacred Mirror was burned in a fire.<ref>Ackroyd, Joyce. (1982). ''Lessons from History: the Tokushi Yoron,'' p. 29.</ref> Whether that mirror was irrevocably lost or not, it is said to be housed today in {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ise Grand Shrine|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ise Grand Shrine|qq=}}, in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], {{ill|Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}},<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cali|first1=Joseph|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J1gEEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA214|title=Shinto Shrines: A Guide to the Sacred Sites of Japan's Ancient Religion|last2=Dougill|first2=John|date=2012-11-30|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3775-4|pages=218|language=en}}</ref> although a lack of public access makes this difficult to verify. Presently, a replica is enshrined in {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Three Palace Sanctuaries|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Palace Sanctuaries|qq=}} of the {{ill|Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial Palace|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tokyo Imperial Palace|qq=}} in Tokyo.<ref name="Denney-2011a" />

== Mythology ==
In {{ill|Shinto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto|qq=}}, the mirror was forged by the deity {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|lt=Ishikoridome|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}; both it and the {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|lt=Yasakani no magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=}}}} were hung from a tree to lure out {{ill|Amaterasu|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=}} from a cave. They were given to Amaterasu's grandson, {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=}}, when he went to pacify Japan along with the sword {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}}}}. From there, the treasures passed into the hands of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial House of Japan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial House of Japan|qq=}}.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&pg=PA4|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|pages=4–5|language=en}}</ref> The descendants of {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|lt=Ishikoridome|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}, the Kagamitsukuri created ceremonial mirrors for the Emperor when the myths were first written.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}

The double shrine complex [[Hinokuma Shrine|Hinokuma Jingu and Kunikakasu Jingu]] holds two mirrors made before this one. Prototype mirrors {{ill|Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|ja|日像鏡・日矛鏡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|1=Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11086052}} respectively.

The researcher Shinsuke Takenaka said according to the legends, Amaterasu told {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=}}: "Serve this mirror as my soul, just as you would serve me, with clean mind and body."<ref name="bbctres"/><ref name="D-2012a">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2012-02-17 |title=The circular mirror: Shinto symbol |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2012/02/18/the-circular-mirror-shinto-symbol/ |access-date=2023-12-12 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Association with the structure of the Department of divinities ==
Yata no Kagami, alongside {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|lt=Yasakani no magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=}}}} were heavily associated with Imperial ritual. Two of the main clans of the [[Department of Divinities]], the Kagamitsukuri, and the Tamatsukuri were descended from the creators of the respective artifacts: {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}, and {{ill|Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=}}. This was a part of a pattern of the clans of the Department of Divinities being descended from significant figures in the myth of Amaterasu in the cave.<ref name="hardacre-2017a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_Q81DQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto: A History|last=Hardacre|first=Helen|date=2017|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-062171-1|language=en}}</ref>{{rp|35}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}} {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}}}} is an exception, likely included to represent the submission of the [[Izumo clan]] to the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial House of Japan]].

In the [[Department of Divinities]] there was this organization.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}

* The {{ill|Inbe clan|Inbe family|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=}} was responsible for managing the procuring materials for rituals and performing abstinence rites.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} and distribution of tribute offerings within the Jingikan..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} claiming descent from Ame no [[Futodama]] no Mikoto..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}
* {{ill|Sarume clan|lt=Sarume clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|en:draft|6=ja|7=猿女君|8=fr|9=Clan Sarume|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|qq=}} women were tasked with performing sacred dances..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} Initially serving as seers and healers, their role evolved to include performing ritual dances, or kagura, during Enthronement Rites and court ceremonies..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} claiming descent from the goddess [[Ame-no-Uzume|Ame no Uzume]] no Mikoto,<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} and {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko Ōkami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko Ōkami|qq=}}. <ref name="picken-2004a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BKAhUVqKFhgC&q=Uzume&pg=PA1|title=Sourcebook in Shinto: Selected Documents|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2004|publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group|isbn=978-0-313-26432-0|language=en}}</ref><ref name="roberts-2009a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Uzume|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}}</ref><ref name="coulter-2013a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VWxekbhM1yEC&dq=Ame-no-Uzume&pg=PT91|title=Encyclopedia of Ancient Deities|last1=Coulter|first1=Charles Russell|last2=Turner|first2=Patricia|date=2013-07-04|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-135-96397-2|language=en}}</ref><ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム">{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9422|access-date=2024-03-18|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}}</ref>
* The Tamatsukuri specialized in the creation of {{ill|Magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama|qq=}}..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} and are descended from {{ill|Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=}}. <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}
* The Kagamitsukuri were known for crafting {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=bronze mirrors|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|qq=}} for use in shrine ceremonies..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} and are descended from {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}. <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}
* The {{ill|Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}} (卜部氏) considered to be of relatively low Rank, carried out divination practices..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}<ref>{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9910|access-date=2024-03-19|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}}</ref> using tortoise shells and deer [[:en:Scapula|scapulae]] <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} later taking the surname {{ill|Urabe clan|lt=Yoshida family|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}} and claiming descent from {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} alongside the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]].<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}

* [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]]: Later known as the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|lt=Fujiwara|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Fujiwara clan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujiwara clan|qq=}}, they specialized in reciting prayers to the Kami, with a divine lineage tracing back to {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}} no Mikoto..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}
** In his book ''Jinja to kodai ōken saishi'' (1989). {{ill|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iwao Ōwa|qq=}} goes on to theorize that the {{Nihongo|[[:en:Ō clan|Ō clan]]|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}} was originally {{Nihongo|ōmi|大忌|"greater taboo (priesthood)"}}, but was usurped by the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]] who were among the "lesser priesthood" (the latter claims descent from the {{Nihongo|[[Inbe clan]]|[[:ja:忌部氏|忌部氏]]}}).<ref name="gakken2">{{cite book|title=神道の本|last=小向|first=正司|publisher=学研|year=1992|series=Books Esoterica|volume=2|pages=76–7}}(zasshi code 66951-07; kyōtsu zasshi code T10-66951-07-1000)</ref>
** Takemikazuchi was originally a local god (''kuni-tsu-kami'') revered by the {{Nihongo|[[:en:Ō clan|Ō clan]]|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}},<ref name="gakken2" /> and was a god of maritime travel.<ref name="gakken2" /> However, the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]] who also has roots in this region, and when they took over control of priestly duties from the Ō clan, they also instituted Takemikazuchi as the Nakatomi clan's [[ujigami]] (clan deity). Or so this is the observation by {{ill|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iwao Ōwa|qq=}}<ref name="gakken2" />

All of these clans are descended from figures who played significant roles in the {{ill|Tenson kōrin|lt=Tenson kōrin|lt=Tenson korin|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tenson korin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenson korin|qq=}} and accompanied Ninigi during his descent, and many of them ({{ill|Sarume clan|lt=Sarume clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|en:draft|6=ja|7=猿女君|8=fr|9=Clan Sarume|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|qq=}}, {{ill|Inbe clan|Inbe family|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=}}, [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]], and {{ill|Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}}) descend from figures ([[Ame-no-Uzume|Ame no Uzume]], [[Futodama]], {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}}, and {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}} respectively) played roles in the myth of Amaterasu in the cave.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}

The {{ill|Mononobe clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Mononobe clan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mononobe clan|qq=}} considered themselves excluded from this, and their ancestor {{ill|Nigihayahi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Nigihayahi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nigihayahi|qq=}} was excluded. For this reason they wrote the {{ill|Kujiki|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kujiki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kujiki|qq=}}. They were highly influential in the development of the department of divinities, but they were not a priestly clan. The Inbe felt their role was minimized so they wrote the {{ill|Kogo Shūi|lt=Kogo Shūi|lt=Kogo Shui|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shui|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shui|qq=}} to improve their position too.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />

== Replicas in contemporary ritual ==
[[File:Masakaki with Mirror and Jewel.jpg|thumb|Right Masakaki at [[Yasaka Shrine]] featuring a Mirror and Magatama]]
[[File:Fukakusa Kaidoguchicho, Fushimi Ward, Kyoto, Kyoto Prefecture 612-0805, Japan - panoramio (1).jpg|thumb|A mirror on an altar at [[Fushimi Inari-taisha]], Yata-no-Kagami is seen as prototypical for the use of mirrors when worshipping other deities.<ref name="degaris-2013a" /><ref name="D-2012a" />]]
{{Main|Masakaki|en:Mirrors in Shinto}}
Replicas of the Imperial regalia of Japan including Yata no Kagami are included in {{ill|Masakaki|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Masakaki|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Masakaki|qq=}} at Shinto shrines.<ref name="d-2015a2">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2015-04-05 |title=The Colours of Shinto (masakaki) |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2015/04/05/the-colours-of-shinto/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref> Masakaki come in sets of two, with the left one containing a replica of {{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}} and the right one containing a replica of Yata no Kagami and {{ill|Yasakani-no-Magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yasakani-no-Magatama|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yasakani-no-Magatama|qq=}}.<ref name="d-2015a2" /> {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|qq=}} are highly significant with Yata no Kagami being seen as prototypical to them.<ref name="degaris-2013a">{{Cite book |last=De_Garis |first=Frederick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hUm0AAAAQBAJ&pg=PA237 |title=We Japanese |date=2013-09-05 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-136-18367-6 |pages=237 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="D-2012a" />

{{Nihongo||{{linktext|八|咫|鏡}}|'''Yata no Kagami'''}} is a sacred {{ill|bronze mirror|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/bronze mirror|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bronze mirror|qq=}} that is part of the {{ill|Imperial Regalia of Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial Regalia of Japan|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Regalia of Japan|qq=}}.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cali|first1=Joseph|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J1gEEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA214|title=Shinto Shrines: A Guide to the Sacred Sites of Japan's Ancient Religion|last2=Dougill|first2=John|date=2012-11-30|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3775-4|pages=218|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Denney-2011a">{{Cite book|last=Denney|first=John W.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9ntpAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA321|title=Respect and Consideration|date=2011|publisher=Lulu.com|isbn=978-0-9568798-0-6|pages=321, 318–326|language=en}}</ref>

== Name and significance ==
The {{transliteration|ja|Yata no Kagami}} represents "wisdom" or "honesty," depending on the source.<ref name="Denney-2011a" /> Its name literally means "The Eight  Mirror," a reference to its size.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Authors|first=Various|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA127|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|pages=127|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Ponsonby-Fane|first=R. A. B.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BY23AwAAQBAJ&pg=PA108|title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines|date=2014-06-03|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-89294-3|pages=108|language=en}}</ref> Mirrors in ancient Japan represented truth because they merely reflected what was shown, and were objects of mystique and reverence (being uncommon items).

According to Shinsuke Takenaka at the Institute of Moralogy, {{transliteration|ja|Yata no Kagami}} is considered the most precious of the three sacred treasures.<ref name="bbctres">{{cite web |title=Akihito and Japan's Imperial Treasures that make a man an emperor |website=BBC |author=Anna Jones |date=27 April 2019 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-47931671 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220324032626/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-47931671 |archive-date=March 24, 2022}}</ref>

== History ==
In the year 1040 ({{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Chōkyū|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Chōkyū|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkyū|qq=}}}} 1, 9th month), the compartment which contained the Sacred Mirror was burned in a fire.<ref>Ackroyd, Joyce. (1982). ''Lessons from History: the Tokushi Yoron,'' p. 29.</ref> Whether that mirror was irrevocably lost or not, it is said to be housed today in {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ise Grand Shrine|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ise Grand Shrine|qq=}}, in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], {{ill|Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}},<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cali|first1=Joseph|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J1gEEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA214|title=Shinto Shrines: A Guide to the Sacred Sites of Japan's Ancient Religion|last2=Dougill|first2=John|date=2012-11-30|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3775-4|pages=218|language=en}}</ref> although a lack of public access makes this difficult to verify. Presently, a replica is enshrined in {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Three Palace Sanctuaries|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Palace Sanctuaries|qq=}} of the {{ill|Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial Palace|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tokyo Imperial Palace|qq=}} in Tokyo.<ref name="Denney-2011a" />

== Mythology ==
In {{ill|Shinto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto|qq=}}, the mirror was forged by the deity {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|lt=Ishikoridome|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}; both it and the {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|lt=Yasakani no magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=}}}} were hung from a tree to lure out {{ill|Amaterasu|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=}} from a cave. They were given to Amaterasu's grandson, {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=}}, when he went to pacify Japan along with the sword {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}}}}. From there, the treasures passed into the hands of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial House of Japan|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial House of Japan|qq=}}.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&pg=PA4|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|pages=4–5|language=en}}</ref> The descendants of {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|lt=Ishikoridome|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}, the Kagamitsukuri created ceremonial mirrors for the Emperor when the myths were first written.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}

The double shrine complex [[Hinokuma Shrine|Hinokuma Jingu and Kunikakasu Jingu]] holds two mirrors made before this one. Prototype mirrors {{ill|Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|ja|日像鏡・日矛鏡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|1=Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11086052}} respectively.

The researcher Shinsuke Takenaka said according to the legends, Amaterasu told {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=}}: "Serve this mirror as my soul, just as you would serve me, with clean mind and body."<ref name="bbctres"/><ref name="D-2012a">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2012-02-17 |title=The circular mirror: Shinto symbol |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2012/02/18/the-circular-mirror-shinto-symbol/ |access-date=2023-12-12 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Association with the structure of the Department of divinities ==
Yata no Kagami, alongside {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|lt=Yasakani no magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=}}}} were heavily associated with Imperial ritual. Two of the main clans of the [[Department of Divinities]], the Kagamitsukuri, and the Tamatsukuri were descended from the creators of the respective artifacts: {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}, and {{ill|Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=}}. This was a part of a pattern of the clans of the Department of Divinities being descended from significant figures in the myth of Amaterasu in the cave.<ref name="hardacre-2017a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_Q81DQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto: A History|last=Hardacre|first=Helen|date=2017|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-062171-1|language=en}}</ref>{{rp|35}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}} {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}}}} is an exception, likely included to represent the submission of the [[Izumo clan]] to the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial House of Japan]].

In the [[Department of Divinities]] there was this organization.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}

* The {{ill|Inbe clan|Inbe family|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=}} was responsible for managing the procuring materials for rituals and performing abstinence rites.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} and distribution of tribute offerings within the Jingikan..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} claiming descent from Ame no [[Futodama]] no Mikoto..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}
* {{ill|Sarume clan|lt=Sarume clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|en:draft|6=ja|7=猿女君|8=fr|9=Clan Sarume|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|qq=}} women were tasked with performing sacred dances..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} Initially serving as seers and healers, their role evolved to include performing ritual dances, or kagura, during Enthronement Rites and court ceremonies..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} claiming descent from the goddess [[Ame-no-Uzume|Ame no Uzume]] no Mikoto,<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} and {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko Ōkami|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko Ōkami|qq=}}. <ref name="picken-2004a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BKAhUVqKFhgC&q=Uzume&pg=PA1|title=Sourcebook in Shinto: Selected Documents|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2004|publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group|isbn=978-0-313-26432-0|language=en}}</ref><ref name="roberts-2009a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Uzume|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}}</ref><ref name="coulter-2013a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VWxekbhM1yEC&dq=Ame-no-Uzume&pg=PT91|title=Encyclopedia of Ancient Deities|last1=Coulter|first1=Charles Russell|last2=Turner|first2=Patricia|date=2013-07-04|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-135-96397-2|language=en}}</ref><ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム">{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9422|access-date=2024-03-18|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}}</ref>
* The Tamatsukuri specialized in the creation of {{ill|Magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama|qq=}}..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} and are descended from {{ill|Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=}}. <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}
* The Kagamitsukuri were known for crafting {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=bronze mirrors|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|qq=}} for use in shrine ceremonies..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} and are descended from {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}. <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}
* The {{ill|Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}} (卜部氏) considered to be of relatively low Rank, carried out divination practices..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}<ref>{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9910|access-date=2024-03-19|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}}</ref> using tortoise shells and deer [[:en:Scapula|scapulae]] <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} later taking the surname {{ill|Urabe clan|lt=Yoshida family|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}} and claiming descent from {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} alongside the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]].<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}

* [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]]: Later known as the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|lt=Fujiwara|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Fujiwara clan|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujiwara clan|qq=}}, they specialized in reciting prayers to the Kami, with a divine lineage tracing back to {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}} no Mikoto..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}
** In his book ''Jinja to kodai ōken saishi'' (1989). {{ill|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iwao Ōwa|qq=}} goes on to theorize that the {{Nihongo|[[:en:Ō clan|Ō clan]]|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}} was originally {{Nihongo|ōmi|大忌|"greater taboo (priesthood)"}}, but was usurped by the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]] who were among the "lesser priesthood" (the latter claims descent from the {{Nihongo|[[Inbe clan]]|[[:ja:忌部氏|忌部氏]]}}).<ref name="gakken2">{{cite book|title=神道の本|last=小向|first=正司|publisher=学研|year=1992|series=Books Esoterica|volume=2|pages=76–7}}(zasshi code 66951-07; kyōtsu zasshi code T10-66951-07-1000)</ref>
** Takemikazuchi was originally a local god (''kuni-tsu-kami'') revered by the {{Nihongo|[[:en:Ō clan|Ō clan]]|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}},<ref name="gakken2" /> and was a god of maritime travel.<ref name="gakken2" /> However, the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]] who also has roots in this region, and when they took over control of priestly duties from the Ō clan, they also instituted Takemikazuchi as the Nakatomi clan's [[ujigami]] (clan deity). Or so this is the observation by {{ill|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iwao Ōwa|qq=}}<ref name="gakken2" />

All of these clans are descended from figures who played significant roles in the {{ill|Tenson kōrin|lt=Tenson kōrin|lt=Tenson korin|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tenson korin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenson korin|qq=}} and accompanied Ninigi during his descent, and many of them ({{ill|Sarume clan|lt=Sarume clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|en:draft|6=ja|7=猿女君|8=fr|9=Clan Sarume|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|qq=}}, {{ill|Inbe clan|Inbe family|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=}}, [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]], and {{ill|Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}}) descend from figures ([[Ame-no-Uzume|Ame no Uzume]], [[Futodama]], {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}}, and {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}} respectively) played roles in the myth of Amaterasu in the cave.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}

The {{ill|Mononobe clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Mononobe clan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mononobe clan|qq=}} considered themselves excluded from this, and their ancestor {{ill|Nigihayahi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Nigihayahi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nigihayahi|qq=}} was excluded. For this reason they wrote the {{ill|Kujiki|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kujiki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kujiki|qq=}}. They were highly influential in the development of the department of divinities, but they were not a priestly clan. The Inbe felt their role was minimized so they wrote the {{ill|Kogo Shūi|lt=Kogo Shūi|lt=Kogo Shui|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shui|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shui|qq=}} to improve their position too.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />

== Replicas in contemporary ritual ==
[[File:Masakaki with Mirror and Jewel.jpg|thumb|Right Masakaki at [[Yasaka Shrine]] featuring a Mirror and Magatama]]
[[File:Fukakusa Kaidoguchicho, Fushimi Ward, Kyoto, Kyoto Prefecture 612-0805, Japan - panoramio (1).jpg|thumb|A mirror on an altar at [[Fushimi Inari-taisha]], Yata-no-Kagami is seen as prototypical for the use of mirrors when worshipping other deities.<ref name="degaris-2013a" /><ref name="D-2012a" />]]
{{Main|Masakaki|en:Mirrors in Shinto}}
Replicas of the Imperial regalia of Japan including Yata no Kagami are included in {{ill|Masakaki|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Masakaki|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Masakaki|qq=}} at Shinto shrines.<ref name="d-2015a2">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2015-04-05 |title=The Colours of Shinto (masakaki) |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2015/04/05/the-colours-of-shinto/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref> Masakaki come in sets of two, with the left one containing a replica of {{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}} and the right one containing a replica of Yata no Kagami and {{ill|Yasakani-no-Magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yasakani-no-Magatama|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yasakani-no-Magatama|qq=}}.<ref name="d-2015a2" /> {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|qq=}} are highly significant with Yata no Kagami being seen as prototypical to them.<ref name="degaris-2013a">{{Cite book |last=De_Garis |first=Frederick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hUm0AAAAQBAJ&pg=PA237 |title=We Japanese |date=2013-09-05 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-136-18367-6 |pages=237 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="D-2012a" />

{{Nihongo||{{linktext|八|咫|鏡}}|'''Yata no Kagami'''}} is a sacred {{ill|bronze mirror|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/bronze mirror|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bronze mirror|qq=}} that is part of the {{ill|Imperial Regalia of Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial Regalia of Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Regalia of Japan|qq=}}.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cali|first1=Joseph|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J1gEEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA214|title=Shinto Shrines: A Guide to the Sacred Sites of Japan's Ancient Religion|last2=Dougill|first2=John|date=2012-11-30|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3775-4|pages=218|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Denney-2011a">{{Cite book|last=Denney|first=John W.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9ntpAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA321|title=Respect and Consideration|date=2011|publisher=Lulu.com|isbn=978-0-9568798-0-6|pages=321, 318–326|language=en}}</ref>

== Name and significance ==
The {{transliteration|ja|Yata no Kagami}} represents "wisdom" or "honesty," depending on the source.<ref name="Denney-2011a" /> Its name literally means "The Eight  Mirror," a reference to its size.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Authors|first=Various|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XEIiEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA127|title=RLE: Japan Mini-Set F: Philosophy and Religion (4 vols)|date=2021-03-18|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90356-4|pages=127|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Ponsonby-Fane|first=R. A. B.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BY23AwAAQBAJ&pg=PA108|title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines|date=2014-06-03|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-89294-3|pages=108|language=en}}</ref> Mirrors in ancient Japan represented truth because they merely reflected what was shown, and were objects of mystique and reverence (being uncommon items).

According to Shinsuke Takenaka at the Institute of Moralogy, {{transliteration|ja|Yata no Kagami}} is considered the most precious of the three sacred treasures.<ref name="bbctres">{{cite web |title=Akihito and Japan's Imperial Treasures that make a man an emperor |website=BBC |author=Anna Jones |date=27 April 2019 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-47931671 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220324032626/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-47931671 |archive-date=March 24, 2022}}</ref>

== History ==
In the year 1040 ({{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Chōkyū|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Chōkyū|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chōkyū|qq=}}}} 1, 9th month), the compartment which contained the Sacred Mirror was burned in a fire.<ref>Ackroyd, Joyce. (1982). ''Lessons from History: the Tokushi Yoron,'' p. 29.</ref> Whether that mirror was irrevocably lost or not, it is said to be housed today in {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ise Grand Shrine|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ise Grand Shrine|qq=}}, in [[:en:Mie Prefecture|Mie Prefecture]], {{ill|Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japan|qq=}},<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cali|first1=Joseph|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J1gEEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA214|title=Shinto Shrines: A Guide to the Sacred Sites of Japan's Ancient Religion|last2=Dougill|first2=John|date=2012-11-30|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-3775-4|pages=218|language=en}}</ref> although a lack of public access makes this difficult to verify. Presently, a replica is enshrined in {{ill|Three Palace Sanctuaries|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Three Palace Sanctuaries|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Three Palace Sanctuaries|qq=}} of the {{ill|Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial Palace|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tokyo Imperial Palace|qq=}} in Tokyo.<ref name="Denney-2011a" />

== Mythology ==
In {{ill|Shinto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinto|qq=}}, the mirror was forged by the deity {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|lt=Ishikoridome|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}; both it and the {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|lt=Yasakani no magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=}}}} were hung from a tree to lure out {{ill|Amaterasu|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=}} from a cave. They were given to Amaterasu's grandson, {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=}}, when he went to pacify Japan along with the sword {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}}}}. From there, the treasures passed into the hands of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Imperial House of Japan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial House of Japan|qq=}}.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&pg=PA4|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|pages=4–5|language=en}}</ref> The descendants of {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|lt=Ishikoridome|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}, the Kagamitsukuri created ceremonial mirrors for the Emperor when the myths were first written.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}

The double shrine complex [[Hinokuma Shrine|Hinokuma Jingu and Kunikakasu Jingu]] holds two mirrors made before this one. Prototype mirrors {{ill|Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|ja|日像鏡・日矛鏡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|1=Higata no Kagami and Hiboko no Kagami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11086052}} respectively.

The researcher Shinsuke Takenaka said according to the legends, Amaterasu told {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|lt=Ninigi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ninigi-no-Mikoto|qq=}}: "Serve this mirror as my soul, just as you would serve me, with clean mind and body."<ref name="bbctres"/><ref name="D-2012a">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2012-02-17 |title=The circular mirror: Shinto symbol |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2012/02/18/the-circular-mirror-shinto-symbol/ |access-date=2023-12-12 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Association with the structure of the Department of divinities ==
Yata no Kagami, alongside {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|lt=Yasakani no magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama#Yasakani no Magatama|qq=}}}} were heavily associated with Imperial ritual. Two of the main clans of the [[Department of Divinities]], the Kagamitsukuri, and the Tamatsukuri were descended from the creators of the respective artifacts: {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}, and {{ill|Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=}}. This was a part of a pattern of the clans of the Department of Divinities being descended from significant figures in the myth of Amaterasu in the cave.<ref name="hardacre-2017a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_Q81DQAAQBAJ|title=Shinto: A History|last=Hardacre|first=Helen|date=2017|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-062171-1|language=en}}</ref>{{rp|35}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}} {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|lt=Kusanagi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}}}} is an exception, likely included to represent the submission of the [[Izumo clan]] to the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial House of Japan]].

In the [[Department of Divinities]] there was this organization.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}

* The {{ill|Inbe clan|Inbe family|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=}} was responsible for managing the procuring materials for rituals and performing abstinence rites.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} and distribution of tribute offerings within the Jingikan..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} claiming descent from Ame no [[Futodama]] no Mikoto..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}
* {{ill|Sarume clan|lt=Sarume clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|en:draft|6=ja|7=猿女君|8=fr|9=Clan Sarume|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|qq=}} women were tasked with performing sacred dances..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} Initially serving as seers and healers, their role evolved to include performing ritual dances, or kagura, during Enthronement Rites and court ceremonies..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} claiming descent from the goddess [[Ame-no-Uzume|Ame no Uzume]] no Mikoto,<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} and {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko Ōkami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko Ōkami|qq=}}. <ref name="picken-2004a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BKAhUVqKFhgC&q=Uzume&pg=PA1|title=Sourcebook in Shinto: Selected Documents|last=Picken|first=Stuart D. B.|date=2004|publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group|isbn=978-0-313-26432-0|language=en}}</ref><ref name="roberts-2009a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xdfgjV2kw6oC&q=Uzume|title=Japanese Mythology A to Z|last=Roberts|first=Jeremy|date=2009|publisher=Infobase Publishing|isbn=978-1-4381-2802-3|language=en}}</ref><ref name="coulter-2013a">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VWxekbhM1yEC&dq=Ame-no-Uzume&pg=PT91|title=Encyclopedia of Ancient Deities|last1=Coulter|first1=Charles Russell|last2=Turner|first2=Patricia|date=2013-07-04|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-135-96397-2|language=en}}</ref><ref name="國學院大學デジタルミュージアム">{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9422|access-date=2024-03-18|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}}</ref>
* The Tamatsukuri specialized in the creation of {{ill|Magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Magatama|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Magatama|qq=}}..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} and are descended from {{ill|Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tamanooya-no-Mikoto|qq=}}. <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}
* The Kagamitsukuri were known for crafting {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|lt=bronze mirrors|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|qq=}} for use in shrine ceremonies..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}} and are descended from {{ill|Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ishikori-dome no Mikoto|qq=}}. <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}
* The {{ill|Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}} (卜部氏) considered to be of relatively low Rank, carried out divination practices..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|35}}<ref>{{Cite web|title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細|url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/id=9910|access-date=2024-03-19|website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム|language=ja}}</ref> using tortoise shells and deer [[:en:Scapula|scapulae]] <ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} later taking the surname {{ill|Urabe clan|lt=Yoshida family|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}} and claiming descent from {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}}.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}} alongside the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]].<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}

* [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]]: Later known as the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|lt=Fujiwara|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Fujiwara clan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujiwara clan|qq=}}, they specialized in reciting prayers to the Kami, with a divine lineage tracing back to {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}} no Mikoto..<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|25-26}}
** In his book ''Jinja to kodai ōken saishi'' (1989). {{ill|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iwao Ōwa|qq=}} goes on to theorize that the {{Nihongo|[[:en:Ō clan|Ō clan]]|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}} was originally {{Nihongo|ōmi|大忌|"greater taboo (priesthood)"}}, but was usurped by the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]] who were among the "lesser priesthood" (the latter claims descent from the {{Nihongo|[[Inbe clan]]|[[:ja:忌部氏|忌部氏]]}}).<ref name="gakken2">{{cite book|title=神道の本|last=小向|first=正司|publisher=学研|year=1992|series=Books Esoterica|volume=2|pages=76–7}}(zasshi code 66951-07; kyōtsu zasshi code T10-66951-07-1000)</ref>
** Takemikazuchi was originally a local god (''kuni-tsu-kami'') revered by the {{Nihongo|[[:en:Ō clan|Ō clan]]|[[:ja:多氏|多氏]]|''Ō no uji''|extra=also written as {{Nihongo2|大氏}}}},<ref name="gakken2" /> and was a god of maritime travel.<ref name="gakken2" /> However, the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]] who also has roots in this region, and when they took over control of priestly duties from the Ō clan, they also instituted Takemikazuchi as the Nakatomi clan's [[ujigami]] (clan deity). Or so this is the observation by {{ill|Iwao Ōwa|ja|大和岩雄|vertical-align=sup|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Iwao Ōwa|qq=}}<ref name="gakken2" />

All of these clans are descended from figures who played significant roles in the {{ill|Tenson kōrin|lt=Tenson kōrin|lt=Tenson korin|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Tenson korin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenson korin|qq=}} and accompanied Ninigi during his descent, and many of them ({{ill|Sarume clan|lt=Sarume clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|en:draft|6=ja|7=猿女君|8=fr|9=Clan Sarume|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarume clan|qq=}}, {{ill|Inbe clan|Inbe family|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inbe clan|qq=}}, [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]], and {{ill|Urabe clan|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|en:draft|Yoshida family|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|fr|Clan Urabe|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}}) descend from figures ([[Ame-no-Uzume|Ame no Uzume]], [[Futodama]], {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}}, and {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}} respectively) played roles in the myth of Amaterasu in the cave.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />{{rp|59}}

The {{ill|Mononobe clan|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Mononobe clan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mononobe clan|qq=}} considered themselves excluded from this, and their ancestor {{ill|Nigihayahi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Nigihayahi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nigihayahi|qq=}} was excluded. For this reason they wrote the {{ill|Kujiki|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kujiki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kujiki|qq=}}. They were highly influential in the development of the department of divinities, but they were not a priestly clan. The Inbe felt their role was minimized so they wrote the {{ill|Kogo Shūi|lt=Kogo Shūi|lt=Kogo Shui|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shui|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogo Shui|qq=}} to improve their position too.<ref name="hardacre-2017a" />

== Replicas in contemporary ritual ==
[[File:Masakaki with Mirror and Jewel.jpg|thumb|Right Masakaki at [[Yasaka Shrine]] featuring a Mirror and Magatama]]
[[File:Fukakusa Kaidoguchicho, Fushimi Ward, Kyoto, Kyoto Prefecture 612-0805, Japan - panoramio (1).jpg|thumb|A mirror on an altar at [[Fushimi Inari-taisha]], Yata-no-Kagami is seen as prototypical for the use of mirrors when worshipping other deities.<ref name="degaris-2013a" /><ref name="D-2012a" />]]
{{Main|Masakaki|en:Mirrors in Shinto}}
Replicas of the Imperial regalia of Japan including Yata no Kagami are included in {{ill|Masakaki|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Masakaki|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Masakaki|qq=}} at Shinto shrines.<ref name="d-2015a2">{{Cite web |last=D |first=John |date=2015-04-05 |title=The Colours of Shinto (masakaki) |url=https://www.greenshinto.com/2015/04/05/the-colours-of-shinto/ |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=Green Shinto |language=en-GB}}</ref> Masakaki come in sets of two, with the left one containing a replica of {{ill|Kusanagi no Tsurugi|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kusanagi no Tsurugi|qq=}} and the right one containing a replica of Yata no Kagami and {{ill|Yasakani-no-Magatama|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Yasakani-no-Magatama|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yasakani-no-Magatama|qq=}}.<ref name="d-2015a2" /> {{ill|Mirrors in Shinto|8=en|simple|User:Immanuelle/Shinto mirror|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mirrors in Shinto|qq=}} are highly significant with Yata no Kagami being seen as prototypical to them.<ref name="degaris-2013a">{{Cite book |last=De_Garis |first=Frederick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hUm0AAAAQBAJ&pg=PA237 |title=We Japanese |date=2013-09-05 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-136-18367-6 |pages=237 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="D-2012a" />
